issues.description: Nil/zero guard boilerplate repeated across ~15-20 accessors instead of captured in one helper
issues.detail: Every getter now opens with the same `var s []T; if x != nil/!x.IsZero() { s = ... }; return seq.NewFixedSlice(...)` pattern. The zero-handling contract should live in one place — a nil-tolerant helper, a guarded-accessor wrapper, or methods on the underlying types — so future getters cannot drift. Right now every author must remember to reproduce the pattern.

issues.description: Two inconsistent nil-zero idioms (`f == nil` vs `IsZero()`) coexist in the same package
issues.detail: `*File` methods guard with `f == nil` while value types like `Type`, `Member`, `Oneof` guard with `!x.IsZero()`. Mixing both shapes forces maintainers to remember which type uses which convention. Pick one canonical predicate (e.g. always `IsZero()`, with `*File.IsZero()` defined as `f == nil`) so the rule is uniform across the IR.

issues.description: Zero-value contract is implicit and enforced only by a reflection-driven test
issues.detail: The PR establishes a real ADT-level contract — zero/nil receivers return zero results — but states it only via `zero_test.go` walking methods reflectively. The promise should be documented at the package or type level (e.g. a doc.go or per-type comment) so the precondition is visible to readers and future method authors, not discovered by a panicking test.

issues.description: `ValueNodeIndex` returns `-1` as an in-band sentinel, leaking absence into the value channel
issues.detail: Returning `-1` for the zero case complects presence with value and forces every caller to branch on the sentinel. `(int, bool)`, an `Optional[int]`, or a separate `HasValueNode()` predicate would keep the contract honest, make the signature self-documenting, and drop the special case from the reflective test.

issues.description: Reflection-based zero test uses name-matched special cases where a small explicit table would be clearer
issues.detail: `testZeroAny` walks `reflect.Type.NumMethod`, special-cases `IsZero`/`ValueNodeIndex`/`Context` by name, and infers accessors from `NumIn==1`, then falls back to any return exposing `Len()`. A boring per-type table of `(name, func(T) any)` would be longer but obvious, catch regressions the heuristic silently passes, and produce clearer failures than a reflect panic.

issues.description: Domain question — whether a zero `*File`/`Type` is legitimate — was answered by patching instead of decided
issues.detail: The PR treats zero receivers as valid domain values everywhere by adding per-accessor guards, but never decides whether that is the contract or whether zero receivers are programmer errors that should be rejected at the boundary. Either model zero once (singleton, value-with-IsZero) or reject it at the boundary and document it — don't carry the ambiguity forward into every future getter.

synthesis.summary: The panel agrees the PR fixes real panics and the intent — making zero a first-class member of each IR type's ADT — is sound. But the execution copy-pastes the same nil-guard boilerplate across ~15-20 accessors, mixes two inconsistent zero idioms (`f == nil` vs `IsZero()`) in one package, and states the contract only through a clever reflection-driven test rather than documented API spec. `ValueNodeIndex`'s `-1` sentinel is a small but avoidable abstraction leak. Ship-able, but a follow-up should unify nil-tolerance into one helper, pick one zero idiom, and document the contract at the type level.
